<reason>CON structured the debate around the conjunctive burden (rates + ethics + distress) and then built a single dilemma that PRO never escaped: a soft default gentle enough to preserve refusal does little to move answers, while any actual gain must come from cases where the family was hesitant and uncertain — so the transplant gain and the ethical/distress cost are drawn from the identical set of cases. PRO's best answer was the "blank registry" reframe (extra organs come from ignorance, not known objection), but CON's closing dismantled it cleanly: a blank registry is evidence of nothing, and PRO's mechanism amounts to scoring the same daughter's same ignorance in the retrieval-favouring direction. On the "measurable" pillar, CON's pressure question forced PRO to concede that the isolating test (default changed, infrastructure constant) "almost never exists," which CON converted into a direct burden failure since the motion claims measurable gain from the shift; CON's Spain-1979-vs-1990s-coordinators, Wales, and Brazil examples are ordinary, plausibly stated background rather than brittle fake precision, and PRO's move of disqualifying each counterexample as "not soft enough" was well punished as walking into the vise. PRO also let CON's foregone-benefit vs wrong-done distinction stand largely unanswered after asserting that opt-in "fails those same people." CON's clipped rebuttal is a modest execution cost, and PRO's answers were properly labelled, but CON still made the decisive comparison clearer and carried it through to the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's response to PRO's blank-registry defence: "Same daughter, same ignorance, opposite outcome" — reframing PRO's alleged gain as uncertainty being rescored rather than a hidden majority preference reaching the table, which welded the transplant gain to the ethical cost and left PRO with no way to keep all three pillars.</best_rebuttal>
